headline: Matinecock Bunker Push Sets Up Execution Rocks for the Fall Run
subhead: Harvest Moon tides are finally stacking bait against the rockpiles from Throgs Neck to Matinecock, and the blitz everybody's waiting on is starting to take shape.
body_markdown:
The question at the bait shop counter this week wasn't whether the fall run was coming — it was why the blitz everybody keeps talking about hadn't broken loose yet on the Western Sound. Fair question. The answer's in the water temps. Kings Point is still holding at 70.9 degrees while New London out east has already slipped to 69.4 — that's a real west-to-east gradient, and it means the warmer western basin is exactly where the bait wants to be right now. Peanut bunker and adult menhaden schools have been staging in that warmer water from Little Neck Bay down through Manhasset Bay, and they're only now starting to push out and get squeezed against structure by the bigger Harvest Moon tides.

We flagged this pattern last week — said the fall bite would build steadily as more bait waves moved through and that blitz-style feeding would pick up as tidal energy built. That's exactly what's setting up now. The moon tides are pulling more water through the pinch points — Throgs Neck, Stepping Stones, the gut between Hart Island and City Island — and that extra current is doing what it always does this time of year: pinning bunker against rock and current seam, and giving the bass and blues a reason to show themselves in daylight instead of just picking at bait after dark.

Execution Rocks has been the most consistent report of the week. The outgoing has been the tide to fish there — start working the structure about an hour into the ebb, when the current really starts to rip off the northeast corner. Snag-and-drop with a live bunker on a fish-finder rig has taken fish, but the better bet for covering water has been a bunker spoon trolled tight to the rockpile, or a 2-ounce white bucktail with a chunk of pork rind bounced along the drop-off on the down-current side. Size has been mixed — plenty of schoolies mixed with mid-20-pound class fish working the bait edges, and a few bigger cows have been reported sitting deeper off the rock on slack before the tide turns hard.

Matinecock Point is holding its usual fall pattern — bunker schools stacking off the point on the last two hours of the ebb, with bass working underneath rather than busting the surface most days. That's typical for this stage of the run; the blitzes come later, once the bait gets nervous and pinned tighter against the beach. For now the better play there is a bucktail worked slow along bottom, 1.5 to 2 ounces depending on the current, white or chartreuse, dragged right through the bait balls rather than cast at them. Bluefish are riding shotgun on every one of those bunker schools — snapper blues are thick in the back bays, Little Neck and Manhasset both, and the bigger cocktail blues have been mixing in at the Throgs Neck Bridge pilings on the last of the incoming, hitting metal and poppers worked fast through the rip.

Fluke have held up better than they usually do this late in September, which tracks with the warmer overall water column. There are still keeper-class fish coming out of 25 to 35 feet off Hart Island and along the channel edge toward Stepping Stones, mostly on white Gulp Swimming Mullets paired with a 3/4-ounce bucktail, dragged slow on the drift with the tide. That bite is going to be the first thing to shut off if a real cold front comes through and knocks the nearshore water down — worth getting after now rather than waiting.

Porgies are doing what they always do this time of year — stacking hard on the reef structure and rockpiles, Execution Rocks and the reef off Sands Point especially, ahead of their own fall exit south. Bloodworms and clam on a hi-lo rig in 20 to 40 feet has been the standard approach, and there's no reason to get fancy with it. Blackfish anglers are starting to gear up, but the tog bite doesn't really turn on in the Western Sound until the water column cools further past the mid-60s — worth scouting your rockpiles now, but don't expect a real tautog bite for another couple weeks. Weakfish remain scarce, which has been the story most of this season — a few incidental fish mixed into the fluke drifts, nothing to plan a trip around.

Looking ahead, the next few days should keep building on this pattern as long as the warm filament holding water in the high 60s to low 70s stays put. Bigger Harvest Moon tides mean sharper current-timed feeding windows — if there's only one window to fish this weekend, make it the start of the ebb at Execution Rocks or the last two hours of outgoing off Matinecock Point, right when the bait gets squeezed hardest. The bigger variable is weather: any real cold front pushing through late this month will start tightening up the fluke bite fast and accelerate the bass moving out of the Sound toward the ocean beaches. Until that happens, the bite here should keep climbing, not fading — this is the leading edge of the fall run, not the peak of it yet.
